evidence.claim: An ancient beach ridge carries nine miles of historic homes.
evidence.quote: This 9-mile byway encompasses the entire length of State Route 254 in Lorain County and passes by more than one hundred historic homes.

evidence.claim: An ancient beach ridge
evidence.quote: this byway follows the northernmost ancient beach ridge across Avon and Shefﬁeld.

evidence.claim: North Ridge Scenic Byway follows the northernmost ancient beach ridge through Sheffield and Avon.
evidence.quote: this byway follows the northernmost ancient beach ridge across Avon and Shefﬁeld.

evidence.claim: Its nine miles take in all of State Route 254 within Lorain County.
evidence.quote: This 9-mile byway encompasses the entire length of State Route 254 in Lorain County

evidence.claim: The Ohio Department of Transportation’s byways brochure highlights more than 100 historic homes, with houses dating to the 1830s.
evidence.quote: With more than 100 historic homes dating back to the 1830s

evidence.claim: In Avon, the older settlement story follows French Creek: Wilbur Cahoon began building a sawmill in 1815 and established a gristmill in 1818.
evidence.quote: In the following year, he began to build a sawmill nearby along French Creek, and in 1818 established a gristmill.

evidence.claim: Wilbur Cahoon began building a sawmill in 1815
evidence.quote: Wilbur Cahoon arrived in Avon in 1814

evidence.claim: His family replaced its log-cabin home with the present house in 1826.
evidence.quote: The log cabin was no longer the Cahoon family home after 1826, when the present house was erected.

evidence.claim: Travel east from Sheffield toward Avon along the ridge.
evidence.quote: this byway follows the northernmost ancient beach ridge across Avon and Shefﬁeld.

evidence.claim: SR 254 is called North Ridge Road at its western end and Detroit Road for most of its course.
evidence.quote: State Route 254 is known as Detroit Road for most of its routing, and as North Ridge Road at its western end.

evidence.claim: In Avon, Detroit Road passes Avon Isle, a sandstone dance pavilion with a low hip roof and columned porches.
evidence.quote: Avon Isle Park Pavilion is a 50 feet (15 m) by 70 feet (21 m) sandstone dance pavilion located on Detroit Road, Avon, Ohio. The dance pavilion is housed in a building featuring several French Colonial revival architecture pieces, including a low hip roof and columned porches.

evidence.claim: The Cahoon house stretches 80 feet long above French Creek, with 12 rooms inside.
evidence.quote: The house is 80 feet (24 m) long with 12 rooms, situated overlooking French Creek.

evidence.claim: Wilbur Cahoon and his family first built a log cabin on their forested land; the present house replaced it in 1826.
evidence.quote: His new land was covered by a forest, and he and his family constructed a log cabin as a temporary shelter.

evidence.claim: the present house replaced it in 1826.
evidence.quote: The log cabin was no longer the Cahoon family home after 1826, when the present house was erected.

evidence.claim: Its Greek Revival design departs from the style’s usual symmetry with an irregular floor plan.
evidence.quote: its floor plan is unusually disorderly, in contrast to the symmetry of typical Greek Revival structures

evidence.claim: From the road, the two-story wooden house has a projecting gable on the left and shuttered windows across much of the front.
evidence.quote: the house is a two-story wooden structure with a protruding gabled section on the left, as seen from the road.  Shuttered windows fill much of the wall space on the facade.

evidence.claim: The building rests on a stone foundation. Its low proportions and irregular plan set it apart from the symmetry usually associated with Greek Revival houses.
evidence.quote: the house is unusually short for its footprint.  Set on a stone foundation

evidence.claim: irregular plan set it apart from the symmetry usually associated with Greek Revival houses.
evidence.quote: its floor plan is unusually disorderly, in contrast to the symmetry of typical Greek Revival structures

evidence.claim: Avon Isle’s sandstone pavilion hosted civic and social events from the 1920s through the 1970s.
evidence.quote: From the 1920s until the 1970s, the venue hosted a variety of civic and social events.

evidence.claim: Avon Isle’s sandstone pavilion
evidence.quote: sandstone dance pavilion located on Detroit Road, Avon, Ohio.

evidence.claim: In its early years, nearby Lorain and Elyria prohibited Sunday dancing.
evidence.quote: During the early years, the larger cities nearby; Lorain and Elyria prohibited dancing on Sunday.

evidence.claim: That restriction helped Avon Isle attract entertainers including Guy Lombardo.
evidence.quote: This allowed Avon Isle to host big-name entertainers like Guy Lombardo.

evidence.claim: The building’s French Colonial revival details include a low hip roof and columned porches.
evidence.quote: The dance pavilion is housed in a building featuring several French Colonial revival architecture pieces, including a low hip roof and columned porches.

evidence.claim: Inside are a stage and kitchenette; the pavilion entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2010.
evidence.quote: features a stage and kitchenette.

evidence.claim: the pavilion entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2010.
evidence.quote: Avon Isle was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2010.

evidence.claim: The pavilion stands on Detroit Road, where the sandstone exterior and porches identify a building designed for gatherings. It also hosted private events.
evidence.quote: It was also available for private events.

evidence.claim: The pavilion stands on Detroit Road, where the sandstone exterior and porches identify a building designed for gatherings.
evidence.quote: sandstone dance pavilion located on Detroit Road, Avon, Ohio.

evidence.claim: Look for the low hip roof and columned porches.
evidence.quote: including a low hip roof and columned porches.

evidence.claim: Avon’s name followed changes in local government.
evidence.quote: In 1818, Township Number 7 was organized and named Xeuma, then later renamed Troy Township.

evidence.claim: Organized as Xeuma in 1818, the township was later called Troy.
evidence.quote: In 1818, Township Number 7 was organized and named Xeuma, then later renamed Troy Township.

evidence.claim: When Lorain County was created in 1824, it became Avon Township, and an Avon post office followed in 1825.
evidence.quote: In 1824, Lorain County was created, and the name was changed to Avon Township. An Avon post office was established in 1825.

evidence.claim: The whole township incorporated as a village in 1917 before becoming the City of Avon in 1961.
evidence.quote: The entire township was incorporated into a village in 1917, and it became the City of Avon in 1961.
